content: Nicotine (oral) is a dependency agent approved by the FDA for managing withdrawal symptoms, including nicotine cravings, associated with smoking cessation. Common side effects include skin irritation, nasal irritation, oral irritation, dizziness, headache, and insomnia. For adults, nicotine lozenges are used to reduce withdrawal symptoms. If you are under 18 years old, consult a doctor before use, as no studies confirm its efficacy in this age group. Before using, read the enclosed User’s Guide for detailed instructions. Start using the lozenge on your quit day. If you smoke your first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking, use a 4 mg lozenge. If you smoke your first cigarette more than 30 minutes after waking, use a 2 mg lozenge. Follow a 12-week schedule for optimal results. Place the lozenge in your mouth and allow it to dissolve slowly over 20-30 minutes. Avoid chewing or swallowing the lozenge. You may experience a warm or tingling sensation. Occasionally move the lozenge from one side of your mouth to the other until it dissolves completely. Do not eat or drink 15 minutes before or during use. To improve your chances of quitting, use at least nine lozenges per day for the first six weeks. Do not use more than one lozenge at a time or continuously, as this may cause hiccups, heartburn, nausea, or other side effects. Do not exceed five lozenges in six hours or 20 lozenges per day. Complete the treatment as directed. If you feel the need to use the lozenge for a longer period to avoid smoking, consult your healthcare provider. There is limited information regarding off-label use of nicotine (oral) in adults, as well as its use in pediatric patients. For pediatric patients, there is no FDA-approved indication or dosage, and off-label use is not well-documented. Nicotine (oral) should be used with caution in specific populations. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, use this medication only under the advice of a healthcare provider. Smoking can harm your child, and it is recommended to attempt quitting without nicotine replacement therapy first. While this medication is considered safer than smoking, the risks to your child are not fully understood. Consult a doctor before use if you have a sodium-restricted diet, heart disease, a recent heart attack, irregular heartbeat, uncontrolled high blood pressure, stomach ulcers, or diabetes. Nicotine can increase heart rate and blood pressure. If you are using a non-nicotine stop-smoking drug or taking prescription medications for depression or asthma, consult a doctor or pharmacist, as your prescription dose may need adjustment. Stop using nicotine lozenges and consult a doctor if you experience mouth problems, persistent indigestion, severe sore throat, irregular heartbeat, palpitations, or symptoms of nicotine overdose such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, diarrhea, weakness, or rapid heartbeat. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets, as it contains enough nicotine to cause harm. If a lozenge needs to be discarded, wrap it in paper and dispose of it in the trash. In case of overdose, seek medical help or contact a Poison Control Center immediately. There is limited information available regarding clinical trial experience, postmarketing experience, drug interactions, and pharmacology of nicotine (oral). Additionally, there is no FDA guidance on its use during pregnancy, labor and delivery, nursing, pediatric use, geriatric use, or in specific populations such as those with renal or hepatic impairment, immunocompromised patients, or specific gender or racial groups. Nicotine lozenges should be administered orally. Monitoring guidelines for this medication are not well-established. There is no information on IV compatibility, chronic overdose, or nonclinical toxicology. Limited data is available on clinical studies, storage, and supply of nicotine (oral). Alcohol-nicotine interactions have not been established, so consult your doctor regarding alcohol use while taking this medication. There is also limited information on brand names and look-alike drug names for nicotine (oral).
